title: From Preservation to Activation: Japan's Next CPTPP Challenge
text:
From Preservation to Activation: Japan's Next CPTPP Challenge

Photo by kokouu via Getty Images

November 18th, 2026

In working with others, Japan has succeeded in preserving the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) after U.S. withdrawal, playing a major leadership role in negotiating the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and signaling its continued commitment to the rules-based trading system. However, Japan now must prioritize and maximize the agreement’s economic value, especially as it continues to face a sluggish domestic economy and a more volatile and fragmented global trading environment.Japan has demonstrated a commitment to free and open trade in a time of increasing uncertainty. Indeed, Japan is credited with salvaging the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), having spearheaded negotiations with remaining members after the United States’ withdrawal in 2017, culminating in the creation of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP). Today, the pressing question is how Tokyo can fully harness and maximize this “gold standard” trade agreement, especially as it faces domestic economic challenges and supply shocks. With CPTPP ministers meeting in Hanoi in late November to build on accession talks, new working groups, and upgrade discussions, Japan’s priorities are threefold: focus on continued CPTPP expansion, ensure businesses are maximizing their use of the agreement, and prioritize CPTPP modernization.Domestically, Japan continues to face a flagging economy. It holds the highest debt to GDP ratio among advanced economies, standing at approximately 200% as of 2026. Japan has also faced inflation and a weak yen, further fueled by its low interest rates. A deepening demographic crisis—with over 30% of the population now aged 65 or older—has additionally fueled concerns over labor shortages and decreasing productivity. This low growth, coupled with recent energy and commodity shocks, has created a myriad of economic hurdles.As supply chains, digital networks, investment flows, standards, and strategic industries grow increasingly interconnected, Japan’s competitiveness will depend in part on its ability to operate at the center of larger economic networks governed by predictable rules. CPTPP can serve as an important platform for building those connections, while also providing a forum for cooperation and coordination on trade resilience and emerging economic risks.Expansion Provides New OpportunitiesAmid growing trade uncertainties—U.S. unpredictability, supply chain disruptions radiating from conflict in the Middle East, and risks associated with China—the CPTPP is increasingly a valuable option for greater trade stability and diversification. The UK accession came into force in 2024, and negotiations with Costa Rica reached substantial conclusion in May 2026. However, on October 28, President Laura Fernández announced that Costa Rica would not sign the accession protocol and would shelve the process. An accession working group is also advancing Uruguay’s application, while the bloc has launched preparatory accession discussions with Indonesia, the Philippines, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Furthermore, CPTPP has established Trade and Investment Dialogues with the EU and ASEAN.For Japan, this offers a multitude of opportunities, especially with Tokyo expected to propose hosting a permanent CPTPP secretariat. In the 2025 CPTPP Quantitative Analysis Report, 15% of Japan’s global merchandise exports were directed to CPTPP partners, with autos and semiconductors among its top exports. Japan also sourced 20% of its total merchandise imports from CPTPP members, including LNG, coal, and copper.Although this is a promising start, to ensure further domestic economic benefits, it is in Tokyo’s interest to strongly support continued expansion. Each additional member enlarges the economic network in which Japanese firms can produce, source, export, and invest under common rules and standards. This is particularly valuable where Japan has existing bilateral agreements—CPTPP can reduce fragmentation by bringing firms into a common framework for rules of origin, services, investment, and digital trade.Pushing to advance the accessions of Indonesia, the Philippines, and the UAE should also be a top priority. Indonesia is Japan’s leading source of processed nickel products, reaping direct benefits for Japan’s EV and battery industries. Japanese multinationals have a strong presence in the Philippines’ manufacturing base, and CPTPP accession would offer deeper production-network integration, especially in electronics manufacturing and automotive assembly. Meanwhile, the UAE supplies over 48.5% of Japan’s crude oil imports as of September 2026 and is one of Japan’s top trading partners in the Middle East. CPTPP accession would bolster energy security while fostering an environment for continued joint ventures in clean energy.Japan already has existing bilateral trade agreements with Indonesia and the Philippines, while negotiations on a Japan-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement concluded in March 2026. This makes the incremental value of CPTPP membership less about establishing preferential trade ties and more about bringing these economies into a larger, collective, high-standard rulebook and production network.Moving forward, Tokyo should actively encourage the applications of South Korea and Thailand. Neither has formally applied, and in October South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung indicated that accession was unlikely during his term. Thailand has signaled renewed interest and accession would bring the country, with whom Japan has an existing FTA and strong trade ties, into CPTPP's robust rules-of-origin, intellectual property (IP), and digital trade standards. Korea’s eventual accession also holds strategic value for Japan’s economy. Tokyo and Seoul do not currently have a bilateral trade agreement, though both are members of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP). CPTPP membership would therefore deepen their existing preferential relationship through more ambitious rules and provide a multilateral network for expanded cooperation.In addition to supporting accessions, Japan should employ CPTPP dialogues with ASEAN and the EU to promote greater interoperability in areas such as digital trade, customs, and regulatory practices. Closer alignment between these major economic frameworks could expand the effective reach of CPTPP rules beyond the agreement’s formal membership. Although Japan currently benefits from bilateral ties with both blocs through the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement and the ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership, the CPTPP dialogues would open further channels for engagement and coordination.Businesses Need to Leverage CPTPP’s BenefitsTo best maximize CPTPP, ensuring businesses are taking advantage of the benefits of the agreement is critical. Despite the tangible benefits for Japanese businesses, FTA and EPA tariff utilization has remained notoriously low in Japan. JETRO’s FTA Survey revealed that while awareness of trade agreements is high at 70%, companies reported difficulties across the board with rules of origin and preparing related documentation. Even among firms that did utilize FTAs, 47% were unaware of the extent of tariff reductions in their export markets. Most critically, a JETRO survey of Japanese firms operating in the Asia-Pacific region placed the CPTPP utilization rate at only 14.3%.Awareness is only part of the challenge—Japanese companies are already reassessing suppliers, investment locations, export markets, and production networks in response to economic security pressures. Further work can be done to help firms identify when CPTPP rules and preferences can lower costs or open opportunities as they make sourcing, export, and investment decisions.Tokyo currently has the foundation to navigate some of these challenges. JETRO’s New Export Nation Consortium (新輸出大国コンソーシアム) helps SMEs leverage CPTPP and other FTAs through seminars and outreach campaigns, while JETRO's EPA consultation desk (EPA相談窓口) and Certificate of Origin Navigator tool (原産地証明ナビ) offer guidance on origin documentation needed to claim CPTPP tariff preferences. However, more work is needed: Japan must shift from providing information to active, firm-level targeting. Instead of waiting for firms to “opt-in” by seeking government consultation services, a more effective strategy would draw on existing survey data to identify and reach out to sectors and businesses that have been underutilizing CPTPP benefits. Japan can additionally look to fellow CPTPP members such as Canada, which integrates CPTPP guidance into a broader, easy to access toolkit that consolidates product- and country-specific tariff finder tools across all Canadian FTAs, as well as databases outlining foreign government procurement opportunities Canadian firms can bid on using CPTPP market access.Furthermore, CPTPP brings advantages beyond tariffs and exports. Tokyo should maximize what CPTPP brings to the table for investment. In 2024, CPTPP economies accounted for 23.9% of inward FDI flows into Japan. In June 2025, the Japanese government set a target of achieving a balance of 120 trillion yen in FDI by 2030. Rules governing national treatment, prohibitions on performance requirements, financial-services market access, and cross-border data flow rules can make Japan a more attractive investment destination for firms from CPTPP partners. Japan could more explicitly incorporate CPTPP partners into its broader inbound investment promotion strategy, particularly in sectors where it is seeking greater capital, technology, and supply-chain integration. Strengthening awareness of CPTPP's investment protections and services access could serve as an important step to draw foreign capital into Japan’s low-growth economy.Modernization Should Be a Top PriorityWith CPTPP soon to mark its eight-year anniversary since coming into force, Japan should play a leading role in efforts to modernize the agreement. CPTPP’s first General Review was completed in 2025, and members have already launched negotiations to update rules covering areas such as digital trade, services, customs, and business facilitation. Importantly, members have also put strengthening supply chain resilience on the agenda and in June established a new ad-hoc working group addressing illegal transshipment and strengthening cooperation on rules of origin and customs administration.Notably, Japan's largest export sectors—autos and tech—now operate in supply chains that are very different from when TPP’s rules of origin were initially negotiated more than a decade ago. Japanese automakers manufacture vehicles across much wider supply chains, while the design and fabrication of chips are now split across many borders. As CPTPP partners look to update the agreement, Japan would benefit from ensuring CPTPP’s full cumulation rules extend to new accession partners without transition gaps or renegotiation delays. Furthermore, Japan should draw on CPTPP’s work on rules of origin to assess whether existing rules continue to reflect modern production networks, particularly in its strategic sectors.Economic security and supply chains are also a key area of reform, especially as Japan continues to face energy shocks from the Iran crisis and critical minerals reliance on China. At the June 2026 CPTPP Commission Meeting, members issued a dedicated Joint Statement on Energy Security and Supply Chains. Although this was a direct response to the current energy crisis, ministers made clear that updating CPTPP provisions to enhance supply chain resilience across the board were top priorities. With members placing growing emphasis on secure and resilient supply chains, Japan should take the lead in kicking off discussions and setting a clear timeline. Japan could also encourage concrete mechanisms for cooperation during future disruptions, including better information sharing, customs coordination, and greater transparency around measures affecting essential goods.Japan’s domestic challenges, alongside a changing trade landscape, make prioritizing and maximizing the CPTPP of utmost importance. Tokyo should continue to advocate for expansion, help Japanese businesses make fuller use of the agreement, and lead efforts to keep CPTPP’s rules relevant to changing patterns of trade and investment.The CPTPP is by no means a fix for Japan’s broader economic challenges. But, if used effectively, it has potential to be more than a traditional trade agreement. At a time when economic competitiveness relies on participation in cross-border production networks, CPTPP offers Japan an opportunity to deepen its position in the supply chains and markets that will shape future growth, while making them more predictable, resilient, and open.

About the Author

Hannah Tsai is currently a master's student at Sciences Po. She was previously a Trade, Investment, & Innovation Intern with ASPI.
